articles.title: A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy
articles.summary: Researchers at Brown University have overcome a major obstacle to creating ultra-low-power computer chips that could help slash the energy demands of AI. Their breakthrough eliminates a long-standing "dead layer" problem that causes promising materials to stop working when made extremely thin. Remarkably, the new technique not only preserves the materials' electrical and magnetic properties at nearly atomic thicknesses but also gives them enhanced magnetic capabilities
articles.content:
A promising new approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence. At the center of the breakthrough is a special class of materials known as multiferroics, which combine electrical and magnetic properties that can be controlled together using extremely small voltages.

These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology. However, a major obstacle has prevented their use in conventional computer chips. When multiferroics are made thin enough to fit inside these devices, they typically lose the electrical and magnetic behavior that makes them valuable. Scientists call this problem the "dead layer" effect.

Researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces extremely thin films of bismuth ferrite, a widely studied multiferroic material, without sacrificing its essential properties. Even more remarkably, the process gives the material new magnetic characteristics that could make it especially useful for future electronics.

"We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer," said Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. "We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want -- down to a few angstroms -- and it's still ferroelectric, and it's still magnetic."

The findings were published in the journal Nature Materials.

Why Multiferroics Could Transform Computer Chips

What makes multiferroics so attractive for computing is the unusual connection between their electrical and magnetic properties. Their atomic structure is made up of repeating units in which positive and negative charges are positioned on opposite sides, creating a property known as electrical polarization.

Applying a small voltage can reverse this polarization, effectively switching the positions of the positive and negative charges. This provides a potential way to store digital information as binary values (ones and zeros) using very little electricity.

Because the material's magnetic behavior is linked to its electrical polarization, the stored information can also be retrieved magnetically. This combination could enable computer memory and logic components that require significantly less energy than existing technologies.

The challenge has been making these materials small enough for practical devices. Modern computer chips require exceptionally thin layers, but multiferroics traditionally stop functioning properly when reduced to such dimensions.

Two separate effects cause this breakdown. First, the material's atomic structure becomes distorted, disrupting the arrangement and chemical environment necessary for its properties to function. Second, internal electric fields interfere with the material's polarization until it can no longer be maintained. Together, these effects destroy both its ferroelectric and magnetic behavior, creating the troublesome dead layer.

How Brown Engineers Eliminated the Dead Layer

To solve the problem, the Brown University team developed a new method for producing thin films of bismuth ferrite.

The researchers deposited the material onto a foundation made of dysprosium scandate, a compound derived from rare earth elements. This underlying material has a crystal structure with slightly smaller dimensions than bismuth ferrite, creating a mismatch between their atomic arrangements.

That mismatch places the bismuth ferrite under compression, helping preserve the atomic structure required for its electrical and magnetic properties to remain intact.

The team also incorporated a second metallic layer designed to counteract unwanted electric fields. By preventing those fields from disrupting the material's electrical polarization, the additional layer addresses the other major cause of the dead layer effect.

Together, these changes allow the bismuth ferrite film to retain its multiferroic properties even when reduced to just a few angstroms in thickness.

But the researchers discovered something else. Rather than simply preserving the material's original capabilities, their approach actually improved its magnetic behavior.

An Unexpected Form of Magnetism

The engineered layers caused the bismuth ferrite to exhibit altermagnetism, an unusual form of magnetism that combines useful characteristics of two more familiar magnetic states: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

This discovery could be particularly important for developing faster and more compact computer components.

"Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out," Caretta said. "The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds -- they can be fast, densely integrated and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout."

In other words, altermagnets offer a potentially valuable combination of speed, compactness, and readable signals. These characteristics could help engineers build computer components that operate efficiently without the interference problems associated with conventional magnetic materials.

The ability to create this magnetic behavior in an exceptionally thin multiferroic film makes the discovery especially promising for future chip designs.

A New Path Toward Energy-Efficient AI Computing

As artificial intelligence continues to drive demand for computing power, developing hardware that consumes less electricity has become an increasingly important goal.

Caretta believes the new findings could help bring multiferroic materials closer to practical use in low-power memory and computing devices. Although the technology still needs further development before it can be incorporated into commercial chips, the research demonstrates that a long-standing materials limitation can be overcome.

It also shows that carefully engineering a material's atomic environment can do more than preserve its existing properties. Under the right conditions, it can produce useful behavior that was not present in the original material.

"We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials," Caretta said. "The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that's useful -- and sometimes even better than what nature gives us."

The research received funding from the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

articles.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
articles.summary: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.
articles.content:
Crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

The findings, published in the journal Science, offer new insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy

To test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent."

The results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

The recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as quickly as primates.

The researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

The impact is broad as it enhances understanding of animal intelligence and brain processing, with detailed experimental context and findings.

articles.title: AI confirms a long-suspected limit on quantum computers’ advantages
articles.summary: An AI-powered proof has rigorously shown that using quantum computers wouldn't have huge advantages for a whole class of mathematical problems, confirming a vastly influential conjecture
articles.content:
An AI-powered proof has rigorously shown that using quantum computers wouldn't have huge advantages for a whole class of mathematical problems, confirming a vastly influential conjecture

Quantum computers can’t significantly outperform standard computers for some calculations mesh cube/Getty Images

A decades-old, vastly influential conjecture about quantum computing has finally been proven – by AI. It confirms that a whole class of mathematical problems wouldn’t be more easily solved by quantum computers.

In 1999, Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin got stuck on a question about when exactly quantum computers could excel over their conventional counterparts.

At this time, researchers knew of at least one example of a problem where the quantum approach outshone all others: Shor’s algorithm for factoring numbers. But they suspected that this hinged on the specific mathematical structure that underlies the factoring problem.

Advertisement

Aaronson wondered whether quantum computers could also win in the opposite case, when the problem contains little to no structure and lots of randomness instead. In 2011, he and Andris Ambainis at the University of Latvia formally conjectured that, in at least one case, the answer was negative – but they couldn’t prove it.

Now, David Turturean at the start-up Physical Superintelligence (PSI) and his colleagues have used Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to provide that proof. This eliminates a whole class of problems from the race to understand what quantum computers are best at.

“It’s a very crisp mathematical question that has consequences for quantum computing, and it has been very hard to solve, to the degree that I had given up on it my myself,” says Ambainis.

“This might be one of the [few] remaining long-standing open questions that are worth pursuing,” says Turturean.

The problem at the heart of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture requires a computer to answer a “yes” or “no” question after being fed a huge but random string of bits, or 1s and 0s. Could a quantum computer get an answer by looking at the string significantly fewer times than a conventional computer would have to? The pair conjectured that a conventional computer could approximate the quantum computer’s performance for most strings and without having to take much longer. More simply, you could get away with not using a quantum computer at all.

Free newsletter Sign up to The Weekly Sign up to newsletter

Importantly, Aaronson and Ambainis translated the statement at the core of their conjecture into the language of polynomials, recasting it as a problem in a different field of pure mathematics. “We didn’t think it would catch on like it did. People who were powerhouses in their own fields and didn’t care about quantum computing got interested,” says Aaronson.

PSI’s breakthrough builds on the work of such mathematicians. Turturean says it took about four days for Fable 5.2, which wasn’t publicly available at the time, to complete the proof, improve and refine it twice, then verify the final version with the proof-checking software Lean. The PSI team then shared the proof with Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan at Stanford University in California, who studied it and wrote an exposition that unravelled its key ingredients.

In a joint statement to New Scientist, they wrote that the new proof meaningfully surpasses all studies that it draws upon. “The proofs are entirely different – and substantially more difficult. Everything is also woven together in a novel way,” they wrote.

Three days after PSI made their proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture public, Supartha Podder at Stony Brook University in New York and his colleagues put forward another, shorter proof of the same thesis, developed with the aid of ChatGPT 5.6 and 6. After four months of building out the framework for their proof, one part of the work by Turturean and his colleagues “supplied the missing ingredient that allowed this approach to succeed”, the researchers wrote in their paper, which was only about seven pages long.

Shachar Lovett at the University of California, San Diego, whose work was one of the key ingredients in the PSI proof, says that this exposition reveals tricks that mathematicians can now learn from and reuse. “This helps us guide our research. What I think is going to come from these AI tools is that now we can maybe ask more ambitious questions,” he says.

But Lovett is cautious about the impact this new work might have on quantum computing, as it is more mathematical than practical, he says. In Aaronson’s view, the weight of the practical implications is also unclear. “This rules out a potential direction where you could look for quantum speed-ups, but it wasn’t a plausible direction anyway,” he says. The glaring question now is where to look for new problems that quantum computers are uniquely positioned to take on.

“This is far from the end of quantum speedups. Instead, it informs us on what types of problems we should consider,” wrote the Stanford team. A similar problem with a shorter or less random input string, or one for which the quantum computer doesn’t give just a “yes” or “no” answer, could still benefit from the quantum approach, they wrote. This leaves tremendously many problems, including simulating industrially relevant molecules and some optimisation problems.

Aaronson says that many of the questions related to quantum information science that are best tackled with mathematics have already been answered by AI, so it is time to formulate some new ones. Matthew Pines at PSI says he and his colleagues now also want to use AI to explore new ideas, instead of just knocking down famous problems. The future will show how successful this can be. “There is some major creative leap needed. I think that’s something where AI is not good yet,” says Ambainis.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant breakthrough where AI has rigorously proven a long-standing conjecture about the limits of quantum computing, clarifying the scope of quantum advantage. This has broad implications for the future direction of quantum computing research, informing scientists on which problems quantum computers can or cannot solve more efficiently. The story highlights a meaningful advancement in technology with potential large-scale impact on computational science and related fields.

articles.personality_title_fr: L’IA prouve une limite clé des capacités des ordinateurs quantiques
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis longtemps, les scientifiques se demandent quand les ordinateurs quantiques peuvent résoudre des problèmes plus rapidement que les ordinateurs classiques. Ils savaient que les ordinateurs quantiques fonctionnaient bien pour certaines tâches, comme la factorisation des nombres, mais soupçonnaient qu’il y avait beaucoup de problèmes où ils n’avaient pas d’avantage.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe dirigée par David Turturean a utilisé un modèle d’IA avancé appelé Fable 5.2 pour prouver une idée ancienne datant de 2011. Cette idée disait que pour certains problèmes aléatoires et complexes, les ordinateurs quantiques ne sont pas beaucoup plus rapides que les ordinateurs classiques. L’IA a mis seulement quelques jours pour créer et vérifier cette preuve, que des experts ont ensuite étudiée et confirmée.

**Impact** – Cette preuve aide les scientifiques à comprendre les vraies limites des ordinateurs quantiques. Elle montre que ces ordinateurs ne vont pas accélérer la résolution de certains types de problèmes, en particulier ceux avec des données aléatoires et des réponses simples oui ou non. Cela permet aux chercheurs de se concentrer sur les problèmes où les ordinateurs quantiques sont vraiment utiles.

Cela pourrait ouvrir de nouvelles voies pour la découverte et l’innovation.

articles.personality_title_es: La IA demuestra un límite clave en lo que pueden hacer las computadoras cuánticas
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante muchos años, los científicos se han preguntado cuándo las computadoras cuánticas pueden resolver problemas más rápido que las computadoras normales. Sabían que las computadoras cuánticas funcionaban bien para algunas tareas, como factorizar números, pero sospechaban que había muchos problemas donde no tenían ventaja.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo liderado por David Turturean usó un modelo avanzado de IA llamado Fable 5.2 para probar una idea antigua de 2011. Esta idea decía que para ciertos problemas aleatorios y complejos, las computadoras cuánticas no son mucho más rápidas que las normales. La IA tardó solo unos días en crear y verificar esta prueba, que luego expertos estudiaron y confirmaron.

**Impacto** – Esta prueba ayuda a los científicos a entender los verdaderos límites de las computadoras cuánticas. Muestra que estas computadoras no acelerarán la solución de algunos tipos de problemas, especialmente los que tienen datos aleatorios y respuestas simples de sí o no. Esto ahorra tiempo y esfuerzo a los investigadores al enfocarse en problemas donde las computadoras cuánticas sí pueden ayudar.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores buscarán nuevos tipos de problemas donde las computadoras cuánticas aún puedan tener ventaja. También planean usar la IA no solo para probar límites, sino para explorar nuevas ideas en computación cuántica. Esto podría abrir nuevos caminos para descubrimientos e innovación.

**Conclusión en una frase** – La IA ayudó a demostrar que las computadoras cuánticas no superarán a las normales en ciertos problemas, guiando la investigación hacia donde realmente existen ventajas cuánticas.
